Computation and reproducibility

Source: vignettes/implementation.Rmd
implementation.Rmd

In this vignette we describe how poolinfo computes its posterior summaries and what evidence there is that they are accurate. We begin with the marginal posterior of the between-site standard deviation and the conditions under which its moments exist, then describe the default quadrature rule and the checks that come with every fit. Next come the second engine and how the two engines compare, the tests’ tolerances, and our reproduction of the numbers in Lee (2026). We end with the derivations behind the parts of the package that go beyond the paper, and a table that maps the paper’s notation to the package’s.

library(poolinfo)

Integrating out the mean

Collect the site estimates τ̂1,…,τ̂J\hat\tau_1, \dots, \hat\tau_J in a vector yy, and let XX be the J×pJ \times p design matrix of the mean model, with rows xj⊤x_j^\top. For a common mean it is a column of ones, and p=1p = 1. Site effects are normal around xj⊤βx_j^\top\beta with standard deviation στ\sigma_\tau, and the estimates are normal around the effects with known variances vjv_j. Write wj=1/(στ2+vj)w_j = 1/(\sigma_\tau^2 + v_j) and W=diag(w1,…,wJ)W = \mathrm{diag}(w_1, \dots, w_J), let b=(X⊤WX)−1X⊤Wyb = (X^\top W X)^{-1} X^\top W y be the weighted least-squares fit, and let Q=(y−Xb)⊤W(y−Xb)Q = (y - Xb)^\top W (y - Xb) be its weighted residual sum of squares. Under a flat prior on β\beta, integrating β\beta out of the likelihood leaves the posterior density of στ\sigma_\tau, up to a constant,

g(στ)=π(στ)|X⊤WX|−1/2∏j(στ2+vj)−1/2exp⁡(−Q/2), g(\sigma_\tau) = \pi(\sigma_\tau)\, |X^\top W X|^{-1/2} \prod_j (\sigma_\tau^2 + v_j)^{-1/2} \exp(-Q/2),

where π\pi is the prior density of στ\sigma_\tau. Apart from π\pi, gg is the restricted likelihood of a random-effects meta-regression at τ2=στ2\tau^2 = \sigma_\tau^2 in metafor’s notation (Harville 1974; Viechtbauer 2010). Under the flat prior on στ\sigma_\tau, then, the posterior density of στ\sigma_\tau peaks at the REML estimate of στ\sigma_\tau. For a common mean, X⊤WX=∑jwjX^\top W X = \sum_j w_j, bb is the precision-weighted mean, and gg is equation (D.2) of Lee (2026). Every diagnostic is a function of στ\sigma_\tau and the vjv_j alone, so each of its posterior summaries is a one-dimensional integral against gg.

Tails and moments

For every στ≥B>0\sigma_\tau \ge B > 0 we have three bounds, where vmaxv_{\max} is the largest vjv_j:

  • exp⁡(−Q/2)≤1\exp(-Q/2) \le 1,
  • ∏j(στ2+vj)−1/2≤στ−J\prod_j (\sigma_\tau^2 + v_j)^{-1/2} \le \sigma_\tau^{-J}, and
  • X⊤WX≥X⊤X/(στ2+vmax)X^\top W X \ge X^\top X / (\sigma_\tau^2 + v_{\max}) in the matrix order.

Together they give

g(στ)≤|X⊤X|−1/2(1+vmax/B2)p/2στp−Jπ(στ),στ≥B, g(\sigma_\tau) \le |X^\top X|^{-1/2} (1 + v_{\max}/B^2)^{p/2}\, \sigma_\tau^{p - J}\, \pi(\sigma_\tau), \qquad \sigma_\tau \ge B,

which for p=1p = 1 is the tail bound of Appendix D.3 of the paper. In the limit the bound is sharp. As στ\sigma_\tau grows, QQ tends to 0 and the ratio of g(στ)g(\sigma_\tau) to στp−Jπ(στ)\sigma_\tau^{p - J} \pi(\sigma_\tau) tends to |X⊤X|−1/2|X^\top X|^{-1/2}, so the tail of gg is that of στp−Jπ(στ)\sigma_\tau^{p - J} \pi(\sigma_\tau).

Suppose the prior density falls off like στ−k\sigma_\tau^{-k}, with k=0k = 0 for the flat prior, k=ν+1k = \nu + 1 for a half-t prior with ν\nu degrees of freedom and k=2k = 2 for the half-Cauchy. Then the posterior mean of στq\sigma_\tau^q is finite exactly when J>q+p+1−kJ > q + p + 1 - k, and the case q=0q = 0 is the condition for a proper posterior. Under the half-normal and uniform priors every moment exists. A flat prior thus needs J≥p+2J \ge p + 2 sites. A proper prior gives a proper posterior with as few as pp sites. With J=pJ = p, however, the fitted values reproduce the estimates whatever στ\sigma_\tau is, gg is a constant times π\pi, and the posterior is the prior. For that reason the package asks for at least p+1p + 1 sites under a proper prior. It integrates only the moments that exist and reports the others as not defined. A posterior mean of a mean-model coefficient requires the first absolute moment of its marginal distribution. Since its conditional standard deviation grows proportionally to στ\sigma_\tau, this requires E(στ)E(\sigma_\tau) to exist: at least p+3p + 3 sites under the flat prior. Its standard deviation requires E(στ2)E(\sigma_\tau^2), hence p+4p + 4 sites. Central intervals remain available when these moments do not exist.

The upper end BB of the integrals is doubled until the bound on the omitted tail of every moment that exists is within its limit, at most 400 times. A moment that exists can still need a larger BB than that when its tail falls off very slowly: the mean of στ\sigma_\tau with 2 sites and a half-t prior with 0.05 degrees of freedom has a tail bound that falls like B−0.05B^{-0.05}. Both engines then stop with an error that names the moment. A prior with a lighter tail avoids it.

Quadrature on panels

The default engine, posterior_control(engine = "nodes"), builds one quadrature rule in στ\sigma_\tau for each fit and uses it for every summary of the fit. Above a lower end σlo\sigma_{\mathrm{lo}} the rule is composite Gauss-Legendre quadrature on t=log⁡στt = \log\sigma_\tau, with the Jacobian dστ=στdtd\sigma_\tau = \sigma_\tau\,dt in its weights. At the start no panel is wider than 0.5 on the log scale. We halve a panel until its 16-point and 32-point rules agree, for the posterior mass and for the second moment when it exists. They agree when they differ by less than 10−1410^{-14} of the total or 64Jϵ64J\epsilon of the panel’s own integral, whichever is larger, where ϵ\epsilon is the machine epsilon. Below the second limit, the rounding error of log⁡g\log g, a sum of JJ terms, no amount of halving brings the two rules closer. Each panel of the final rule has 32 nodes.

Below σlo\sigma_{\mathrm{lo}} the rule is a single 32-point Gauss-Legendre panel in στ\sigma_\tau itself. Panels on the log scale cannot reach 0, yet under every prior of sd_prior() the posterior density of στ\sigma_\tau is positive there, and roughly g(0)σlog(0)\,\sigma_{\mathrm{lo}} of the unnormalized mass lies between 0 and σlo\sigma_{\mathrm{lo}}. We set σlo\sigma_{\mathrm{lo}} to e−8e^{-8} times the smallest standard error, or times the scale of a proper prior or the upper limit of a uniform prior if that is smaller. Below it στ2\sigma_\tau^2 is less than e−16e^{-16} times every vjv_j, and neither the likelihood nor the prior changes much.

Under a uniform prior the upper end BB is the prior’s upper limit. Otherwise BB starts well beyond the spread of the estimates and the standard errors, and is doubled until the bounds of the previous section, divided by the mass below BB, meet two limits. The bound on the mass must fall below 10−1210^{-12}, and the bound on E(στq)E(\sigma_\tau^q) below 10−10GM(v)q/210^{-10}\,\mathrm{GM}(v)^{q/2}, for each of q=1,2,4q = 1, 2, 4 whose moment exists. Dividing by the mass below BB rather than the whole makes the bounds conservative. With the factor GM(v)q/2\mathrm{GM}(v)^{q/2} the limits change with the units of the estimates, so the rule does not depend on them. We compare the bounds with their limits on the log scale, where no power of στ\sigma_\tau overflows. Within a panel, the distribution function is the integral of the Legendre series that matches the density at the panel’s 32 nodes, and the quantiles are its roots.

We use the passing outcome of the credit recovery study as the example. Each fit stores its rule as fit$rule.

fit <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, data = ocrs)
rule <- fit$rule
data.frame(nodes = length(rule$sigma), panels = length(rule$edges) - 1,
           sigma_lo = rule$sigma_lo, B = rule$upper)
#>   nodes panels     sigma_lo        B
#> 1   800     24 2.596037e-05 3.630941

The rule has 800 nodes, 32 in each of the 24 panels above σlo\sigma_{\mathrm{lo}}, here 2.6e-05, and 32 below it. Its upper end, B=3.63B = 3.63, is 28 times GM(v)=0.128\sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)} = 0.128 and 14 times the 97.5% quantile of στ\sigma_\tau.

Numerical checks

Every fit carries checks of its integration, which check_numerics() lists.

check_numerics(fit)[, c("check", "value", "limit", "status")]
#>                                                             check        value
#> 1     normalizing constant, rule against halved panels (relative) 0.000000e+00
#> 2            E(I) and E(H), rule against halved panels (relative) 1.654837e-16
#> 3           normalizing constant, lower end moved down (relative) 0.000000e+00
#> 4                  E(I) and E(H), lower end moved down (relative) 0.000000e+00
#> 5                               mass beyond the upper end (bound) 9.678885e-32
#> 6 E(sigma_tau^1) beyond the upper end, over sqrt(GM(v))^1 (bound) 2.844392e-30
#> 7 E(sigma_tau^2) beyond the upper end, over sqrt(GM(v))^2 (bound) 8.368938e-29
#> 8 E(sigma_tau^4) beyond the upper end, over sqrt(GM(v))^4 (bound) 7.273389e-26
#> 9            turning points of H at two resolutions (logit scale) 6.938894e-17
#>   limit status
#> 1 1e-10     ok
#> 2 1e-10     ok
#> 3 1e-10     ok
#> 4 1e-10     ok
#> 5 1e-12     ok
#> 6 1e-10     ok
#> 7 1e-10     ok
#> 8 1e-10     ok
#> 9 1e-07     ok

The first four rows compare the rule with two others. Halving every panel tests whether the panels are fine enough, and moving the lower end down to σlo/2\sigma_{\mathrm{lo}}/2 tests the treatment of the mass near 0. Each compares the normalizing constants and the posterior means of II and HH, as relative differences, with the limit 10−1010^{-10}, or 64Jϵ64J\epsilon if that is larger. The next rows bound the mass beyond BB and, for the orders that exist, the part of E(στq)E(\sigma_\tau^q) beyond BB, divided by GM(v)q\sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)}^q. The last row compares HH’s turning point, on the logit scale, as found by two scans of different resolution. For this fit the largest relative difference between rules is 1.7e-16, and the tail bounds are at most 7.3e-26. Since BB is doubled only until the tail bounds pass, in other fits those rows can come close to their limits. A value outside its limit makes reliability_posterior() give a warning that points to check_numerics().

The adaptive engine

posterior_control(engine = "adaptive") computes each posterior mean, probability and quantile as a separate integral with stats::integrate(), as in the computation of Lee (2026). On a finite range integrate() uses the adaptive Gauss-Kronrod routine of QUADPACK (Piessens et al. 1983), which starts from a single 21-point rule over the whole range. When the integrand is concentrated in a small part of a long range, that first rule can miss it, and integrate() returns 0 with an error estimate of 0:

integrate(dnorm, 0, 1e4, mean = 60, sd = 0.5)
#> 0 with absolute error < 0

Its true value is 1. Splitting the range so that the peak falls in a piece of moderate length avoids the failure. So the adaptive engine splits the range at GM(v)\sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)}, as the paper did, and also at 9 points spread evenly on the log scale over the stretch where the density of log⁡στ\log\sigma_\tau exceeds e−70e^{-70} times its largest value. Besides these extra splits, it differs from the paper’s computation in two ways. Its integrals end at the node rule’s upper end BB, while the paper’s run to infinity. And it takes the posterior standard deviations, and the intervals of the site effects and of the coefficients, from a node rule. Each integrand is scaled before it is integrated so that integrate()’s absolute tolerance acts as a relative one. For the eight schools, the tests check that multiplying the estimates and the standard errors by factors from 10−10010^{-100} to 1010010^{100} changes the posterior means of the diagnostics by less than 10−910^{-9}, relative, under both engines.

The two engines use the same kernel gg, the same upper end BB with the tail bounds that fix it, and the same formulas for the diagnostics. The adaptive engine also takes its standard deviations from a node rule. So their agreement checks the integration over [0,B][0, B], by panels and Legendre series on one side and by adaptive subdivision on the other. The kernel and the formulas are checked against metafor’s restricted likelihood, against brute-force integrals, and against reference values computed for Lee (2026) with separate code that integrates to infinity. The node rule is the default because it is faster: a single rule serves every summary of a fit, while the adaptive engine integrates each summary, and each site, separately.

Tolerances

Below are the tolerances of the tests, kept in tests/testthat/helper-tolerances.R. The first row is for identities of the profile algebra, which are true in exact arithmetic. The others govern two comparisons, with full-precision reference values computed for Lee (2026) and between the two engines. In the fourth row, xx is the value being compared.

Quantity Tolerance
identities of the profile algebra 10−1210^{-12}
II, S‾\bar S, HH, SjS_j and probabilities 10−910^{-9}, absolute
JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}} 10−910^{-9}, relative
στ\sigma_\tau, the mean effect, site means and standard deviations 10−9max⁡{GM(v),|x|}10^{-9}\max\{\sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)}, \lvert x\rvert\}
E(στ2)E(\sigma_\tau^2) and its quantiles 10−810^{-8}, relative
II at E(στ2)E(\sigma_\tau^2) 10−810^{-8}, absolute
normalizing constant 10−1010^{-10}, relative
turning point of HH (logit scale) 10−710^{-7}

For E(στ2)E(\sigma_\tau^2) the tolerance is looser, because the posterior tail of στ2\sigma_\tau^2 is heavy. With 5 sites under the flat prior, its variance does not exist. Brute-force integrals are less accurate than either engine, and the tests that compare with them use looser tolerances:

  • 10−810^{-8} for posterior means under proper priors, and for the means and standard deviations of the site effects
  • 10−710^{-7}, relative, for E(στ)E(\sigma_\tau) when the prior’s scale is far below the standard errors
  • 10−610^{-6} for the conditional moments of the site effects under a mean model, against a joint normal computation
  • 10−410^{-4} for the kernel of a mean model, against a two-dimensional integral over β\beta

Reproducing the paper

The data set ocrs has the inputs of the credit recovery study’s 6 analyses in Lee (2026). They are course passing in all 32 sites, in the 13 Algebra 1 sites and in the 19 English 9 sites, passing with covariates, credits earned, and passing as a log odds ratio. The first five are the rows of the paper’s Table 5 and Table G.1, and the last is the log-odds row of Table G.2. We fit each with both engines.

algebra <- ocrs$subject == "Algebra 1"
analyses <- list(
  Pooled = fit,
  `Algebra 1` = reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se,
                                      data = ocrs[algebra, ]),
  `English 9` = reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se,
                                      data = ocrs[!algebra, ]),
  Adjusted = reliability_posterior(estimate_adjusted, se = se_adjusted,
                                   data = ocrs),
  Credits = reliability_posterior(estimate_credits, se = se_credits,
                                  data = ocrs),
  `Log odds` = reliability_posterior(log_odds_ratio, se = se_log_odds_ratio,
                                     data = ocrs)
)
adaptive <- lapply(analyses, update,
                   control = posterior_control(engine = "adaptive"))

We tabulate the node rule’s posterior means and interval ends to four decimals.

tab <- as.data.frame(compare_profiles(.list = analyses))
cols <- c("I", "I_lower", "I_upper", "mean", "H", "H_lower", "H_upper",
          "J_eff")
cbind(tab["analysis"], round(tab[cols], 4))
#>    analysis      I I_lower I_upper   mean      H H_lower H_upper   J_eff
#> 1    Pooled 0.6709  0.4974  0.8122 0.6635 0.0253  0.0185  0.0289 31.1704
#> 2 Algebra 1 0.6293  0.2939  0.8654 0.6253 0.0164  0.0086  0.0196 12.6976
#> 3 English 9 0.7074  0.4932  0.8678 0.6983 0.0284  0.0176  0.0342 18.4945
#> 4  Adjusted 0.6522  0.4736  0.8003 0.6444 0.0279  0.0205  0.0317 31.0343
#> 5   Credits 0.3181  0.0220  0.5972 0.3271 0.0285  0.0031  0.0376 28.7982
#> 6  Log odds 0.5302  0.2532  0.7434 0.5296 0.0346  0.0263  0.0367 30.1660

Rounded as the paper rounds them, the first five rows are the entries of its Table 5, and the last row gives II and HH in the log-odds row of its Table G.2. The other numbers in the paper’s Tables G.1 and G.2 for these analyses, such as the posterior mean of στ\sigma_\tau, II at E(στ2)E(\sigma_\tau^2) and Pr(I > 1/2), round to the paper’s entries in the same way. Pooled passing, for example, has I=0.6709I = 0.6709 with the interval from 0.4974 to 0.8122, which Table 5 prints as .67 [.50, .81].

For each analysis we then find the largest difference between the two engines over the posterior means and the ends of the intervals, in four groups:

  • the bounded diagnostics and the probability that II exceeds 1/2
  • JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}}, relative to its value
  • στ\sigma_\tau and the mean effect, in units of GM(v)\sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)}
  • στ2\sigma_\tau^2, relative to its value
differences <- function(a, b) {
  pa <- profile_summary(a)
  pb <- profile_summary(b)
  at <- function(p, q) unlist(p[p$quantity == q, c("mean", "lower", "upper")])
  gap <- function(q) abs(at(pa, q) - at(pb, q))
  rel <- function(q) abs(at(pa, q) / at(pb, q) - 1)
  c(bounded = max(gap("I"), gap("mean"), gap("H"),
                  abs(prob_above(a) - prob_above(b))),
    J_eff = max(rel("J_eff")),
    effect_scale = max(gap("sigma_tau"), gap("effect_mean")) /
      exp(mean(log(site_table(a)$se))),
    sigma_tau2 = max(rel("sigma_tau2")))
}
engines <- t(mapply(differences, analyses, adaptive))
signif(engines, 2)
#>           bounded   J_eff effect_scale sigma_tau2
#> Pooled    8.9e-16 2.2e-16      5.2e-15    5.1e-15
#> Algebra 1 1.1e-15 2.2e-16      8.3e-15    6.6e-15
#> English 9 3.3e-14 6.3e-15      2.5e-13    2.0e-13
#> Adjusted  2.3e-15 4.4e-16      1.1e-14    1.1e-14
#> Credits   6.2e-15 2.7e-15      1.9e-14    2.5e-13
#> Log odds  6.1e-16 2.2e-16      9.9e-16    3.1e-15

Across the 6 analyses the engines differ by at most 3.4e-14 on the bounded diagnostics, 6.4e-15 relative on JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}}, 2.6e-13 of GM(v)\sqrt{\mathrm{GM}(v)} on στ\sigma_\tau and the mean effect, and 2.6e-13 relative on στ2\sigma_\tau^2, at least 3 orders of magnitude inside the tolerances.

The package’s tests make the same fits and compare them, under both engines, with full-precision reference values computed for Lee (2026) and stored in tests/testthat/cases/ocrs-reference.rds. For each analysis they compare 24 of the 28 stored summaries, including every number for these analyses that the paper’s tables print, within the tolerances above. In the same file, tests/testthat/test-posterior-reference.R, they do this for 6 simulated data sets whose reference values are stored in tests/testthat/cases/boundary-cases.rds. Slower tests in tests/testthat/test-engines-slow.R compare the engines on the 6 analyses and on 500 random data sets of 3 to 200 sites. In these data sets the sampling variances spread over several orders of magnitude, and about a tenth of them have an outlying estimate. The slow tests also run the node rule alone on 400 extreme data sets, with up to 10,000 sites and ratios of sampling variances up to 10810^8, and require finite, ordered summaries and every check within its limit. These tests take several minutes and run only when the environment variable POOLINFO_SLOW is "true". From the package’s source directory, this command runs them:

POOLINFO_SLOW=true Rscript -e 'devtools::test(filter = "engines-slow")'

Beyond the paper

The paper’s computations are for a common mean and the flat prior. The package goes beyond them in five places, and for each we give the derivation and the tests that check it.

Mean models

With β\beta integrated out, site jj’s effect given στ\sigma_\tau has posterior mean Sjτ̂j+(1−Sj)xj⊤bS_j\hat\tau_j + (1 - S_j)\,x_j^\top b and variance στ2(1−Sj)+(1−Sj)2xj⊤(X⊤WX)−1xj\sigma_\tau^2(1 - S_j) + (1 - S_j)^2\, x_j^\top (X^\top W X)^{-1} x_j, where xj⊤(X⊤WX)−1xj=hjj/wjx_j^\top (X^\top W X)^{-1} x_j = h_{jj}/w_j and hjjh_{jj} is the jjth diagonal element of W1/2XW^{1/2}X’s hat matrix. The tests compare gg with metafor’s restricted likelihood for p=1,2,3p = 1, 2, 3 and with a two-dimensional brute-force integral over β\beta. They also compare the conditional moments of the site effects with a joint normal computation in which β\beta has a very diffuse normal prior.

Proper priors

The half-normal, half-t, half-Cauchy and uniform priors of sd_prior() enter gg through π(στ)\pi(\sigma_\tau). The tail bound above contains π(στ)\pi(\sigma_\tau), and the integral of the bound times στq\sigma_\tau^q beyond BB has a closed form, or a closed-form bound, for each prior. It is a power of BB for the flat and half-t priors, a normal tail probability or an upper incomplete gamma function for the half-normal, and 0 for the uniform prior, whose upper limit is BB. We test the posteriors under each prior against brute-force integrals, and each bound against the integral that it bounds.

Intervals for H

With the vjv_j fixed, logitSj=log⁡στ2−log⁡vj\mathrm{logit}\, S_j = \log\sigma_\tau^2 - \log v_j, so the centered logits Δj=log⁡{GM(v)/vj}\Delta_j = \log\{\mathrm{GM}(v)/v_j\} do not depend on στ\sigma_\tau, which acts only through m=logitI=log⁡{στ2/GM(v)}m = \mathrm{logit}\, I = \log\{\sigma_\tau^2/\mathrm{GM}(v)\}. Along this path dH/dm=S‾−IdH/dm = \bar S - I(Lee 2026, Proposition 2(i)), and differentiating once more gives

d2HdI2=−J−1∑j(Sj−I)2{I(1−I)}2, \frac{d^2 H}{dI^2} = -\frac{J^{-1}\sum_j (S_j - I)^2}{\{I(1 - I)\}^2},

which is negative unless all the vjv_j are equal, and then HH and the gap are 0 for every στ\sigma_\tau. With unequal sampling variances, HH is therefore strictly concave in II and has a single peak, where S‾=I\bar S = I. Lee (2026) locates the peak by scans at two resolutions; since there is only one, the package finds the single root of S‾−I\bar S - I and keeps a scan as a check. For 0<h<Hmax0 < h < H_{\max} there are two values σ1(h)<σ2(h)\sigma_1(h) < \sigma_2(h) of στ\sigma_\tau at which H=hH = h, and H≤hH \le h if and only if στ≤σ1(h)\sigma_\tau \le \sigma_1(h) or στ≥σ2(h)\sigma_\tau \ge \sigma_2(h). With FF the posterior distribution function of στ\sigma_\tau,

P(H≤h)=F{σ1(h)}+1−F{σ2(h)}. P(H \le h) = F\{\sigma_1(h)\} + 1 - F\{\sigma_2(h)\}.

The package finds σ1(h)\sigma_1(h) and σ2(h)\sigma_2(h) by Newton’s method in mm, kept inside a bracket by bisection, with the exact derivative S‾−I\bar S - I, and solves this equation for the quantiles of HH. Near a constant profile, or when II is close to 1, S‾\bar S and II agree in most of their digits, and their plain difference loses those digits. To keep them, the package uses the exact identity Sj−I=−(1−I)Sj{exp⁡(−Δj)−1}S_j - I = -(1 - I)\, S_j\{\exp(-\Delta_j) - 1\}, evaluated with expm1(), and subtracts I(1−I)I(1 - I) times the mean of the computed Δj\Delta_j, which rounding moves slightly away from 0.

Draws from other software

The diagnostics depend on the draws only through στ\sigma_\tau, so draws of στ\sigma_\tau from any algorithm that targets the same model and prior give the same posterior summaries, up to Monte Carlo error. reliability_draws() computes their Monte Carlo standard errors with the effective sample sizes of posterior::ess_mean() (Vehtari et al. 2021). Its site summaries average over the draws of the mean rather than integrate the mean out. In the tests, draws from profile_draws() go to reliability_draws(), whose posterior means must be within 4.5 Monte Carlo standard errors of the integrals.

You can compare a brms fit (Bürkner 2017) of the eight schools with the integrals in the same way. In brms a standard deviation is bounded below at 0, so a Student t prior of class sd is the half-t of sd_prior(), and an empty prior on the intercept makes the prior on the mean flat.

library(brms)
fit_brms <- brm(
  estimate | se(se) ~ 1 + (1 | school), data = eight_schools,
  prior = c(prior("", class = Intercept),
            prior(student_t(3, 0, 10), class = sd)),
  chains = 4, iter = 4000, seed = 1, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99)
)
from_brms <- reliability_draws(fit_brms)
from_brms
exact <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, site = school,
                               data = eight_schools,
                               prior = sd_prior("half_t", scale = 10, df = 3))
exact

The posterior means that from_brms prints should differ from those of exact by no more than a few of the Monte Carlo standard errors printed beside them.

Confidence intervals for the between-site variance

In metafor’s notation στ2\sigma_\tau^2 is τ2\tau^2. Suppose an interval CC covers στ2\sigma_\tau^2 with probability 1−α1 - \alpha. Because II increases with στ2\sigma_\tau^2, the interval between II at the ends of CC covers II with the same probability, and so does the interval for S‾\bar S. So does the interval for JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}} when the sampling variances differ; when they are all equal, Jeff=JJ_{\mathrm{eff}} = J for every στ\sigma_\tau and its interval is the single value JJ. HH is not monotone, and map_tau2_interval() reports its smallest and largest values over CC instead, using HH’s peak when the peak lies inside CC. That range contains HH whenever CC contains στ2\sigma_\tau^2, so its coverage is at least 1−α1 - \alpha.

For a metafor fit, CC is the Q-profile interval of Viechtbauer (2007) for the model of the fit, moderators included. With Q(στ2)Q(\sigma_\tau^2) the weighted residual sum of squares of the estimates at στ2\sigma_\tau^2 (the generalized QQ statistic), its lower end solves Q(στ2)=χJ−p,1−α/22Q(\sigma_\tau^2) = \chi^2_{J-p,\,1-\alpha/2} and its upper end Q(στ2)=χJ−p,α/22Q(\sigma_\tau^2) = \chi^2_{J-p,\,\alpha/2}, where χJ−p,q2\chi^2_{J-p,\,q} is the qq quantile; an end is 0 when Q(0)Q(0) is already below its quantile. map_tau2_interval() solves these equations itself, for log⁡(στ2/GM(v))\log(\sigma_\tau^2 / \mathrm{GM}(v)), so that the ends do not depend on the units of the effects and an end close to 0 has the same relative precision as one far above it. It does so for every estimator of metafor, also for GENQ and GENQM fits, whose own confint() uses another method. The tests compare the mapped ends with the profiles at the ends of the interval, and the upper end for HH with HH’s peak when the peak lies inside the interval. For the eight schools they also compare the end found with that of confint() run with a wider limit. We fit the eight schools with metafor and map its interval.

reml <- metafor::rma(estimate, sei = se, data = eight_schools,
                     method = "REML")
confint(reml)
#> 
#>        estimate  ci.lb     ci.ub 
#> tau^2    0.0000 0.0000 >100.0000 
#> tau      0.0000 0.0000  >10.0000 
#> I^2(%)   0.0000 0.0000  >42.3703 
#> H^2      1.0000 1.0000   >1.7352
mapped <- map_tau2_interval(reml)
attr(mapped, "interval")
#> estimate    lower    upper 
#>   0.0000   0.0000 270.3672
mapped
#>   functional estimate    lower      upper
#> 1          I 0.000000 0.000000 0.64736618
#> 2       mean 0.000000 0.000000 0.64068042
#> 3      J_eff 6.817468 6.817468 7.76992874
#> 4          H 0.000000 0.000000 0.02836966

metafor reports the upper end as above 100, and the interval that is mapped ends at 270.4. Through II the difference is large, since II is 0.40 at 100 and 0.65 at 270.4.
